visuals.title_latex: A word problem becomes calculus through a translation pipeline
visuals.caption_latex: Strong application work moves from the situation to named variables, then to an equation, then to a derivative, and finally back to a sentence in the original context.
visuals.learning_purpose: This diagram establishes the standard architecture for every substantial word problem in Unit 2B. It should appear in the unit hub, be referenced by related-rates and optimization lessons, and become the structure of interactive solution forms. The goal is to make modeling visible as a sequence of decisions rather than a magical jump from prose to symbols.
visuals.long_description: Strong application work moves from the situation to named variables, then to an equation, then to a derivative, and finally back to a sentence in the original context. The derivative sits in the middle of the work. Most application errors happen before it, when variables or relationships are chosen badly, or after it, when a correct number is reported without units or meaning. The final check may send you back to the model if the answer is physically impossible.
visuals.reading_guide_latex: The derivative sits in the middle of the work. Most application errors happen before it, when variables or relationships are chosen badly, or after it, when a correct number is reported without units or meaning. The final check may send you back to the model if the answer is physically impossible.
visuals.editorial_brief_latex:
\textbf{Instructional purpose.} This diagram establishes the standard architecture for every substantial word problem in Unit 2B. It should appear in the unit hub, be referenced by related-rates and optimization lessons, and become the structure of interactive solution forms. The goal is to make modeling visible as a sequence of decisions rather than a magical jump from prose to symbols.

\textbf{Composition.} Use five main stages and a final model-check node. The dashed return arrow is essential: a model is not automatically valid merely because its derivative was computed correctly. Each node should contain an action and not simply a noun. Keep units visible in the variables and interpretation stages.

\textbf{Web behavior.} Application pages should implement this as a persistent stepper. Learners first name quantities and units, then select or write a relationship, then differentiate. The system should not reveal the equation immediately after a wrong first attempt; instead, it should offer a diagram or targeted hint. At the interpretation stage, require a sentence template containing quantity, time/input, sign, and units.

\textbf{Accessibility.} Provide the six stages as an ordered list. On mobile, stack vertically. Alt text must include the feedback loop: ``After checking the result, revise the assumptions if the answer is implausible.'' Color should reinforce but never replace numbering and labels.

visuals.title_latex: Position, velocity, and acceleration are three synchronized views of motion
visuals.caption_latex: Position tells where the object is. Velocity tells how position changes. Acceleration tells how velocity changes. Aligning the graphs by time makes changes of direction and speeding behavior visible.
visuals.learning_purpose: This stacked graph is the core visual for motion interpretation. It should replace the common practice of teaching three formulas in isolation. Students need to see that position, velocity, and acceleration share the same time axis and describe different layers of the same event.
visuals.long_description: Position tells where the object is. Velocity tells how position changes. Acceleration tells how velocity changes. Aligning the graphs by time makes changes of direction and speeding behavior visible. Follow one time vertically through all three panels. Zeros of velocity correspond to horizontal tangents and possible direction changes in position. The sign of velocity tells direction. The sign of acceleration tells whether velocity is moving upward or downward, but speeding up depends on the signs of both velocity and acceleration.
visuals.reading_guide_latex: Follow one time vertically through all three panels. Zeros of velocity correspond to horizontal tangents and possible direction changes in position. The sign of velocity tells direction. The sign of acceleration tells whether velocity is moving upward or downward, but speeding up depends on the signs of both velocity and acceleration.
visuals.editorial_brief_latex:
\textbf{Instructional purpose.} This stacked graph is the core visual for motion interpretation. It should replace the common practice of teaching three formulas in isolation. Students need to see that position, velocity, and acceleration share the same time axis and describe different layers of the same event.

\textbf{Mathematical specification.} Use $s(t)=t^3-6t^2+9t$, $v(t)=3t^2-12t+9$, and $a(t)=6t-12$ on $0\le t\le5$. Align panel widths and horizontal scales exactly. Mark or optionally annotate $t=1$, $t=2$, and $t=3$, where important sign or turning behavior occurs.

\textbf{Web behavior.} A shared vertical cursor should display all three values and a plain-language motion sentence, such as ``moving left and slowing down.'' A play control may move the particle along a number line while the cursor advances, but animation must be pausable and frame-step accessible. Include a toggle for sign strips beneath $v$ and $a$.

\textbf{Accessibility.} Alt text should summarize intervals of direction and acceleration, not attempt to list every plotted point. The three equations must be available as text. On mobile, preserve the vertical stack and synchronized cursor.

visuals.title_latex: Speeding up and slowing down depend on two signs
visuals.caption_latex: An object speeds up when velocity and acceleration have the same sign and slows down when their signs differ. The rule follows from whether the magnitude $|v|$ is moving away from or toward zero.
visuals.learning_purpose: This matrix targets one of the most persistent motion misconceptions: confusing negative velocity with deceleration. The key idea is magnitude. The labels ``more negative'' and ``toward zero'' make that mechanism explicit.
visuals.long_description: An object speeds up when velocity and acceleration have the same sign and slows down when their signs differ. The rule follows from whether the magnitude |v| is moving away from or toward zero. Negative velocity does not mean slowing down. It means motion in the negative direction. If acceleration is also negative, the velocity becomes more negative and the speed increases. The table organizes all four sign combinations so you can reason rather than guess from the word ``negative.''
visuals.reading_guide_latex: Negative velocity does not mean slowing down. It means motion in the negative direction. If acceleration is also negative, the velocity becomes more negative and the speed increases. The table organizes all four sign combinations so you can reason rather than guess from the word ``negative.''
visuals.editorial_brief_latex:
\textbf{Instructional purpose.} This matrix targets one of the most persistent motion misconceptions: confusing negative velocity with deceleration. The key idea is magnitude. The labels ``more negative'' and ``toward zero'' make that mechanism explicit.

\textbf{Composition.} Use velocity signs as rows and acceleration signs as columns. Each interior cell states speeding/slowing and includes a short verbal explanation. Color is supportive only; the words must carry the meaning. The footnote states the general rule using $|v|$.

\textbf{Web behavior.} Present random pairs of velocity and acceleration values. A number-line animation should show the velocity point moving under the influence of acceleration for a short time. The learner predicts speeding or slowing before revealing the motion. Avoid a car animation that implies rightward motion is inherently positive; a number line is more mathematically honest.

\textbf{Accessibility.} Implement as a real HTML table with row and column headers. Alt text may summarize the same-sign/opposite-sign rule. On mobile, the matrix may remain a table with horizontal scrolling rather than being converted to four unlabeled cards.

visuals.title_latex: translating between $f$ and $f'$
visuals.caption_latex: The zeros and signs of \(f'(x)=3x^2-3\) encode the increasing and decreasing behavior of \(f(x)=x^3-3x\).
visuals.learning_purpose: Train bidirectional translation between the local slopes of a function and the values and signs of its derivative.
visuals.long_description: The zeros and signs of (f'(x)=3x 2-3 ) encode the increasing and decreasing behavior of (f(x)=x 3-3x ).
visuals.reading_guide_latex: See the adjacent lesson prose and the detailed editorial brief.
visuals.editorial_brief_latex:
\textbf{Purpose.} This paired graph trains bidirectional translation: slopes on $f$ become heights on $f'$, and signs on $f'$ become increasing or decreasing intervals on $f$. It should not be presented as a matching puzzle based on overall shape.

\textbf{Composition.} Use $f(x)=x^3-3x$ and $f'(x)=3x^2-3$ with aligned horizontal axes. Mark $x=-1$ and $x=1$ in both panels. In the original graph these are horizontal tangents and local extrema; in the derivative graph they are zeros. Shade or annotate the intervals where $f'$ is positive and negative in the web edition.

\textbf{Interaction.} A shared cursor should report $f(a)$, $f'(a)$, and a short sentence such as ``the original graph is decreasing here.'' A tangent line on the upper/original graph should update with the cursor. Include a reverse activity in which the derivative graph is shown first and the learner sketches possible behavior of the original up to a vertical shift.

\textbf{Accessibility.} Alt text should list the derivative sign intervals and corresponding behavior. On mobile, stack the panels and preserve aligned x-scales. Use direct formulas and different line patterns.

visuals.title_latex: Finite data produce derivative estimates, not exact derivatives
visuals.caption_latex: Forward, backward, and central differences use different neighboring measurements. Symmetric data often make the central estimate more accurate, but measurement noise and spacing still matter.
visuals.learning_purpose: This visual distinguishes mathematical derivatives from data-derived estimates and opens discussion of uncertainty. It should reinforce that units and measurement spacing are part of the answer.
visuals.long_description: Forward, backward, and central differences use different neighboring measurements. Symmetric data often make the central estimate more accurate, but measurement noise and spacing still matter. At the target time t=3 , the lines use measurements on different sides. The estimates are close but not identical because the temperature curve is not perfectly linear. A derivative estimated from a table should therefore be reported with appropriate precision and with the units degrees Celsius per minute.
visuals.reading_guide_latex: At the target time $t=3$, the lines use measurements on different sides. The estimates are close but not identical because the temperature curve is not perfectly linear. A derivative estimated from a table should therefore be reported with appropriate precision and with the units degrees Celsius per minute.
visuals.editorial_brief_latex:
\textbf{Instructional purpose.} This visual distinguishes mathematical derivatives from data-derived estimates and opens discussion of uncertainty. It should reinforce that units and measurement spacing are part of the answer.

\textbf{Composition.} Plot a smooth curve through a small temperature data set and highlight three measurements around $t=3$. Draw backward, forward, and central secants with distinct patterns. The central line should be visually emphasized but not labeled ``correct.''

\textbf{Web behavior.} Let users change the data spacing and add controlled noise. Display each finite-difference estimate and compare it with the derivative of an underlying hidden model when the ``show benchmark'' toggle is enabled. Ask the learner to choose a sensible number of reported decimal places.

\textbf{Accessibility.} Provide the data table adjacent to the graph in the web version. Alt text should identify the target time and the three secant choices. Line styles must remain distinct in grayscale.

visuals.title_latex: square-root curve and its linearization
visuals.caption_latex: Near \(x=4\), the graph of \(\sqrt x\) is nearly indistinguishable from its tangent line.
visuals.learning_purpose: Make local linearity visible by comparing a function with its tangent approximation while the viewing window and target point change.
visuals.long_description: Near (x=4 ), the graph of ( x ) is nearly indistinguishable from its tangent line.
visuals.reading_guide_latex: See the adjacent lesson prose and the detailed editorial brief.
visuals.editorial_brief_latex:
\textbf{Purpose.} The graph introduces local linearity before the approximation formula becomes routine. The learner should see both that the tangent is not the curve and that the difference becomes difficult to detect near the contact point.

\textbf{Composition.} Plot $f(x)=\sqrt{x}$ and $L(x)=2+\frac14(x-4)$, mark $(4,2)$, and preserve a wide view. The web edition should pair this with a linked magnified view whose window is controlled by a zoom slider. Display the signed error $f(x)-L(x)$ and the absolute error.

\textbf{Interaction.} The learner moves a target point, predicts whether the tangent overestimates or underestimates based on concavity, and then reveals the true value. A second slider shrinks $|x-4|$ and shows the error relative to the displacement. Avoid displaying so many decimals that the numerical readout becomes the lesson.

\textbf{Accessibility.} Alt text should name both formulas, the contact point, and the fact that the tangent lies above the concave-down square-root curve near the point. On mobile, stack wide and zoomed views and put the error table below.

visuals.title_latex: Linearization replaces a difficult local curve with an easy line
visuals.caption_latex: Near $x=a$, the tangent line starts at the known value $f(a)$ and changes at the known rate $f'(a)$. The horizontal move $\Delta x$ creates the estimated vertical move $f'(a)\Delta x$.
visuals.learning_purpose: This visual should connect the line formula to an incremental mental model. Many students can substitute into L(x) but cannot explain what the terms mean. The two measurement arrows make f(a)+f'(a) x visible.
visuals.long_description: Near x=a , the tangent line starts at the known value f(a) and changes at the known rate f'(a) . The horizontal move x creates the estimated vertical move f'(a) x . For f(x)= x near a=4 , the known point is (4,2) and the slope is 1/4 . Moving from 4 to 4.5 gives x=0.5 , so the tangent predicts a vertical change of (1/4)(0.5)=0.125 . The estimate is therefore 2.125 .
visuals.reading_guide_latex: For $f(x)=\sqrt{x}$ near $a=4$, the known point is $(4,2)$ and the slope is $1/4$. Moving from $4$ to $4.5$ gives $\Delta x=0.5$, so the tangent predicts a vertical change of $(1/4)(0.5)=0.125$. The estimate is therefore $2.125$.
visuals.editorial_brief_latex:
\textbf{Instructional purpose.} This visual should connect the line formula to an incremental mental model. Many students can substitute into $L(x)$ but cannot explain what the terms mean. The two measurement arrows make $f(a)+f'(a)\Delta x$ visible.

\textbf{Mathematical specification.} Use $f(x)=\sqrt{x}$ at $a=4$ and estimate at $x=4.5$. Plot the curve and tangent $L(x)=2+\frac14(x-4)$. Mark the known point and the tangent estimate. The actual curve value may be marked with an open symbol in the interactive version so the error can be seen.

\textbf{Web behavior.} Allow a draggable target $x$. Display $\Delta x$, predicted $\Delta y$, linear estimate, true value, and error. A zoom slider should show the error shrinking. Ask the learner to predict over- or underestimation from concavity before revealing the true value.

\textbf{Accessibility.} Alt text should narrate the horizontal and vertical moves and give the computed estimate. Use arrow labels and not color alone. On mobile, position the numeric calculation beneath the graph.

visuals.title_latex: Differentials separate the actual change from the tangent-line estimate
visuals.caption_latex: The curve produces the actual output change $\Delta y$. The tangent line produces the differential $dy=f'(x)dx$. Their vertical gap is the approximation error.
visuals.learning_purpose: This visual prevents the common equation dy= y from being treated as exact. It should reinforce that dy belongs to the tangent model and y belongs to the original function.
visuals.long_description: The curve produces the actual output change y . The tangent line produces the differential dy=f'(x)dx . Their vertical gap is the approximation error. Starting at x=1 , the input changes by dx=0.7 . The tangent predicts dy=2(0.7)=1.4 , while the curve actually changes by y=1.89 . The two quantities are close only when the input change is sufficiently small; they are not identical by definition.
visuals.reading_guide_latex: Starting at $x=1$, the input changes by $dx=0.7$. The tangent predicts $dy=2(0.7)=1.4$, while the curve actually changes by $\Delta y=1.89$. The two quantities are close only when the input change is sufficiently small; they are not identical by definition.
visuals.editorial_brief_latex:
\textbf{Instructional purpose.} This visual prevents the common equation $dy=\Delta y$ from being treated as exact. It should reinforce that $dy$ belongs to the tangent model and $\Delta y$ belongs to the original function.

\textbf{Mathematical specification.} Use $f(x)=x^2$ at $x=1$ with $dx=0.7$. Plot the tangent $y=2x-1$. Mark the actual point on the curve and the tangent estimate at the new input. Label horizontal change, predicted vertical change, actual vertical change, and error.

\textbf{Web behavior.} Let the learner shrink $dx$ and observe the error. Display $\Delta y-dy$ and the relative error. A checkbox may switch between positive and negative $dx$ to show that the geometry works in both directions.

\textbf{Accessibility.} Alt text should explicitly distinguish actual and approximate changes. Use different arrow positions and labels so colors are unnecessary. On mobile, enlarge the local region and put equations below.

visuals.title_latex: Newton's method turns tangent lines into improved root estimates
visuals.caption_latex: At each estimate, the tangent line is easier to solve than the curve. Its $x$-intercept becomes the next estimate. Repeating the construction can converge rapidly to a root.
visuals.learning_purpose: The visual should make the iteration formula geometrically inevitable. Students should see that -f(x n)/f'(x n) is the horizontal correction obtained from the tangent line, not an arbitrary numerical recipe.
visuals.long_description: At each estimate, the tangent line is easier to solve than the curve. Its x -intercept becomes the next estimate. Repeating the construction can converge rapidly to a root. The first tangent begins at (2,2) and crosses the axis at x 1=1.5 . The next tangent begins on the curve at x 1 and crosses near x 2=1.4167 . The intercepts move toward 2 . Each step uses x n+1 =x n-f(x n)/f'(x n) .
visuals.reading_guide_latex: The first tangent begins at $(2,2)$ and crosses the axis at $x_1=1.5$. The next tangent begins on the curve at $x_1$ and crosses near $x_2=1.4167$. The intercepts move toward $\sqrt2$. Each step uses $x_{n+1}=x_n-f(x_n)/f'(x_n)$.
visuals.editorial_brief_latex:
\textbf{Instructional purpose.} The visual should make the iteration formula geometrically inevitable. Students should see that $-f(x_n)/f'(x_n)$ is the horizontal correction obtained from the tangent line, not an arbitrary numerical recipe.

\textbf{Mathematical specification.} Use $f(x)=x^2-2$ with $x_0=2$. Draw at least the first two tangent lines and mark their axis intercepts. The final root need not be marked exactly; the sequence should visibly approach it. Use labels $x_0,x_1,x_2$.

\textbf{Web behavior.} Provide step, reset, and starting-value controls. Display a table of $n$, $x_n$, $f(x_n)$, and absolute error when the true root is known. Include deliberately poor starting values to demonstrate failure or slow convergence. Never autoplay without controls.

\textbf{Accessibility.} Alt text should narrate the two tangent steps and list the estimates. Keyboard controls are required. On mobile, show one iteration at a time with a persistent history table.

visuals.title_latex: Newton iteration tool
visuals.caption_latex: Newton iteration tool
visuals.learning_purpose: Turn Newton’s method into an inspectable tangent-line iteration, including convergence, divergence, derivative-zero warnings, and cycles.
visuals.long_description: A coordinate graph shows a function, the current iterate, its tangent line, and the next x-intercept. A synchronized table lists each iterate, residual, and error when a reference root is known. Previous steps remain as a light trail. Controls allow step, undo, reset, and starting-value changes. Failure states such as a nearly horizontal tangent, divergence, or a two-cycle are explained in text and equations.
visuals.reading_guide_latex: See the adjacent lesson prose and the detailed editorial brief.
visuals.editorial_brief_latex:
\textbf{Purpose.} This specification extends the static Newton visual into a complete numerical laboratory. It should make each tangent construction inspectable and make failure modes available rather than presenting only a perfectly convergent example.

\textbf{Required views.} Show the curve, current point, tangent, next intercept, and complete iteration table. Preserve prior intercepts as a light trail so the sequence is visible. Include a residual column $|f(x_n)|$ and, when a benchmark root is known, an error column.

\textbf{Controls and feedback.} Provide step, undo, reset, and starting-value controls. Never autoplay by default. If $f'(x_n)$ is zero or very small, show a specific warning. Include examples that converge to different roots, diverge, or cycle. A textual explanation must accompany every failure state.

\textbf{Accessibility.} Every graphical step must also appear as an equation and table row. Keyboard operation is mandatory. On mobile, show one tangent step at a time with the table immediately below.

visuals.title_latex: Related rates use one geometric relationship at one frozen instant
visuals.caption_latex: The quantities change with time, but the equation relating them is geometric or physical. Differentiate the relationship first, then substitute the measurements and rates from the instant of interest.
visuals.learning_purpose: This visual should be reused verbatim across every related-rates lesson so students internalize a stable method. The ``frozen instant'' language belongs in the accompanying prose: the diagram at one moment supplies values, while derivatives describe how those values are changing at that moment.

Differentiate the relationship first, then substitute the measurements and rates from the instant of interest. The most important order is ``relationship, differentiate, substitute.'' If you insert snapshot numbers too early, variables disappear and the derivative has nothing left to describe. The diagram also reminds you that related-rates answers need a sign and units, not merely a magnitude.

If you insert snapshot numbers too early, variables disappear and the derivative has nothing left to describe. The diagram also reminds you that related-rates answers need a sign and units, not merely a magnitude.

\textbf{Instructional purpose.} This visual should be reused verbatim across every related-rates lesson so students internalize a stable method. visuals.title_latex: Sliding ladder geometry
visuals.caption_latex: The wall, ground, and ladder form a right triangle. The fixed ladder length gives $x^2+y^2=L^2$, while $dx/dt$ and $dy/dt$ describe the horizontal and vertical endpoint speeds.
visuals.learning_purpose: The diagram should support variable selection and sign reasoning before any numbers are used. It must show that L is constant while x and y vary. Arrows make the direction conventions explicit.
visuals.long_description: The wall, ground, and ladder form a right triangle. The fixed ladder length gives x 2+y 2=L 2 , while dx/dt and dy/dt describe the horizontal and vertical endpoint speeds. As the foot moves away from the wall, x increases. Because the ladder length stays fixed, the top must move downward, so y decreases. Differentiating x 2+y 2=L 2 gives 2x dx/dt+2y dy/dt=0 , which already predicts opposite signs.
visuals.reading_guide_latex: As the foot moves away from the wall, $x$ increases. Because the ladder length stays fixed, the top must move downward, so $y$ decreases. Differentiating $x^2+y^2=L^2$ gives $2x\,dx/dt+2y\,dy/dt=0$, which already predicts opposite signs.
visuals.editorial_brief_latex:
\textbf{Instructional purpose.} The diagram should support variable selection and sign reasoning before any numbers are used. It must show that $L$ is constant while $x$ and $y$ vary. Arrows make the direction conventions explicit.

\textbf{Composition.} Draw a vertical wall, horizontal ground, right-angle marker, and ladder. Label $x$, $y$, and fixed length $L$. Add motion arrows at the endpoints with signed rate labels. Keep the geometry simple; decorative textures or a cartoon worker add no mathematical value.

\textbf{Web behavior.} Drag the foot horizontally while maintaining fixed ladder length. Update $x$, $y$, and the tangent rate relationship. Let users specify $dx/dt$ and calculate $dy/dt$. The top endpoint should move continuously and the Pythagorean equation should remain visible.

\textbf{Accessibility.} Alt text should describe the right triangle, fixed hypotenuse, and endpoint directions. The interactive controls need keyboard alternatives. On mobile, use a square drawing area and place rate inputs below.

visuals.title_latex: A conical tank combines volume and similar-triangle relationships
visuals.caption_latex: The water volume depends on both radius and depth. Similar triangles provide $r/h=R/H$, allowing the two changing dimensions to be expressed using one variable before differentiating.
visuals.learning_purpose: This visual addresses the two-equation structure of many volume problems. Students often differentiate the volume formula while leaving both r and h unknown, then discover they have too many rates. The similar-triangle labels should make the reduction step visible.
visuals.long_description: The water volume depends on both radius and depth. Similar triangles provide r/h=R/H , allowing the two changing dimensions to be expressed using one variable before differentiating. The large cone and the water cone have the same shape, so r/h=R/H . That relationship is not optional bookkeeping; it eliminates one changing variable from V=(1/3) r 2h . Only after that substitution is the volume differentiated with respect to time.
visuals.reading_guide_latex: The large cone and the water cone have the same shape, so $r/h=R/H$. That relationship is not optional bookkeeping; it eliminates one changing variable from $V=(1/3)\pi r^2h$. Only after that substitution is the volume differentiated with respect to time.
visuals.editorial_brief_latex:
\textbf{Instructional purpose.} This visual addresses the two-equation structure of many volume problems. Students often differentiate the volume formula while leaving both $r$ and $h$ unknown, then discover they have too many rates. The similar-triangle labels should make the reduction step visible.

\textbf{Composition.} Draw the full cone and a smaller similar water cone sharing the vertex. Label full dimensions $R,H$ and water dimensions $r,h$. Show the water level as an ellipse and add an upward depth-rate arrow. Use consistent radius labels from the central axis to the side.

\textbf{Web behavior.} A water-level slider should resize the inner cone while preserving similarity. Display the ratios $r/h$ and $R/H$. Let users choose whether to eliminate $r$ or $h$, then differentiate the resulting one-variable volume expression.

\textbf{Accessibility.} Alt text should state that the water region is a smaller similar cone and list both equations. On mobile, avoid overly shallow ellipses that become invisible. Provide the geometry as SVG with labeled text elements, not a raster image.

visuals.title_latex: Shadow problems are similar-triangle problems
visuals.caption_latex: A light, a person, and the shadow tip form one large triangle. The person's height and shadow form a smaller triangle. Their proportional sides connect walking speed to shadow growth.
visuals.learning_purpose: The visual should prevent variable ambiguity. Students frequently use the same symbol for the person's distance from the light and the shadow length, or forget that the shadow tip is farther from the light by their sum.
visuals.long_description: A light, a person, and the shadow tip form one large triangle. The person's height and shadow form a smaller triangle. Their proportional sides connect walking speed to shadow growth. The large triangle has height H and base x+s . The smaller triangle has height h and base s . Similarity gives H/(x+s)=h/s . Notice that the shadow tip's distance from the light is x+s , not just s .

\textbf{Instructional purpose.} The visual should prevent variable ambiguity. Students frequently use the same symbol for the person's distance from the light and the shadow length, or forget that the shadow tip is farther from the light by their sum.

visuals.title_latex: A derivative sign chart turns algebra into a graph story
visuals.caption_latex: Critical numbers divide the domain into intervals. Testing the sign of $f'$ on each interval determines whether the original function rises or falls and classifies sign changes.
visuals.learning_purpose: The chart should bridge symbolic factor signs and graph behavior. It is a reusable component for increasing/decreasing intervals, the first derivative test, and optimization verification.
visuals.long_description: Critical numbers divide the domain into intervals. Testing the sign of f' on each interval determines whether the original function rises or falls and classifies sign changes. A positive derivative means the original function increases; a negative derivative means it decreases. At x=-2 , the sign changes from positive to negative, so f has a local maximum. At x=1 , the sign changes from negative to positive, so f has a local minimum.

visuals.title_latex: Concavity describes how slopes change
visuals.caption_latex: On a concave-up curve, tangent slopes increase and tangent lines lie locally below the graph. On a concave-down curve, slopes decrease and tangents lie locally above.

In the right panel, slopes progress from positive to zero to negative, so they are decreasing and f''<0 . Concavity is about the trend of slopes, not whether the function itself is above or below the axis.

visuals.title_latex: An optimization diagram separates the objective from the constraint
visuals.caption_latex: For a rectangle with fixed perimeter, width and length cannot vary independently. The constraint eliminates one variable; the objective function then measures the area to maximize.
visuals.learning_purpose: This visual should establish the anatomy of optimization: quantity to optimize, restriction, feasible variables, and one-variable objective. It should be reused in later geometry examples with different shapes.
visuals.long_description: For a rectangle with fixed perimeter, width and length cannot vary independently. The constraint eliminates one variable; the objective function then measures the area to maximize. The area formula A=xy is the objective. The perimeter equation is the constraint. Solving the constraint for y gives A(x)=x(P/2-x) , a one-variable function that can be differentiated. The diagram keeps the two jobs separate.
visuals.reading_guide_latex: The area formula $A=xy$ is the objective. The perimeter equation is the constraint. Solving the constraint for $y$ gives $A(x)=x(P/2-x)$, a one-variable function that can be differentiated. The diagram keeps the two jobs separate.
visuals.editorial_brief_latex:
\textbf{Instructional purpose.} This visual should establish the anatomy of optimization: quantity to optimize, restriction, feasible variables, and one-variable objective. It should be reused in later geometry examples with different shapes.

\textbf{Composition.} Draw a labeled rectangle with area inside and place the perimeter constraint in a separate card connected by an arrow. The separate card matters because students often differentiate the constraint instead of the objective or never use the constraint to reduce variables.

\textbf{Web behavior.} Let a slider vary $x$ while preserving perimeter. The rectangle should reshape, and an area graph should update simultaneously. The learner predicts the maximizing shape before differentiating. Show the feasible interval $0<x<P/2$.

\textbf{Accessibility.} Alt text should state the objective and constraint. The interactive slider needs keyboard support and numeric entry. On mobile, stack the rectangle above the constraint and area graph.

visuals.title_latex: Marginal quantities are slopes of total quantities
visuals.caption_latex: Marginal cost and marginal revenue are derivative graphs. Profit increases where marginal revenue exceeds marginal cost and is stationary where they are equal.

visuals.long_description: Marginal cost and marginal revenue are derivative graphs. Profit increases where marginal revenue exceeds marginal cost and is stationary where they are equal. After q=6 , marginal cost is larger, so additional production reduces profit in this model.

visuals.caption_latex: The rule applies only after a quotient limit is verified to have the form $0/0$ or $\infty/\infty$. Other forms must first be transformed or handled by simpler methods.

visuals.long_description: The rule applies only after a quotient limit is verified to have the form 0/0 or / . Other forms must first be transformed or handled by simpler methods. You do not use L'Hopital's Rule because a fraction looks complicated. First evaluate the numerator and denominator limits separately. If the verified form is not 0/0 or / , differentiating top and bottom is not justified. After applying the rule, test the new form again.

visuals.caption_latex: Products become quotients, differences are combined or rationalized, and powers are handled by logarithms. The transformation creates a quotient of type $0/0$ or $\infty/\infty$.

visuals.long_description: Products become quotients, differences are combined or rationalized, and powers are handled by logarithms. The transformation creates a quotient of type 0/0 or / . visuals.title_latex: Elasticity measures how relative input error is amplified
visuals.caption_latex: Absolute sensitivity uses $f'(x)$. Relative sensitivity uses the dimensionless factor $E(x)=x f'(x)/f(x)$, which predicts the approximate percentage output change caused by a one-percent input change.
visuals.learning_purpose: This visual distinguishes absolute derivative sensitivity from relative conditioning. It should help students understand why a derivative of 1000 is not automatically ``large'' and why percentage comparisons often provide the meaningful scale.
visuals.long_description: Absolute sensitivity uses f'(x) . Relative sensitivity uses the dimensionless factor E(x)=x f'(x)/f(x) , which predicts the approximate percentage output change caused by a one-percent input change. The first box measures error as a fraction of the input rather than in raw units. Elasticity multiplies that fraction. The result is a fractional output error, so the comparison works across quantities with different units and scales. Large |E(x)| warns that small relative input errors may be strongly amplified.
visuals.reading_guide_latex: The first box measures error as a fraction of the input rather than in raw units. Elasticity multiplies that fraction. The result is a fractional output error, so the comparison works across quantities with different units and scales. Large $|E(x)|$ warns that small relative input errors may be strongly amplified.
visuals.editorial_brief_latex:
\textbf{Instructional purpose.} This visual distinguishes absolute derivative sensitivity from relative conditioning. It should help students understand why a derivative of $1000$ is not automatically ``large'' and why percentage comparisons often provide the meaningful scale.

\textbf{Exact composition and examples.} Use a three-stage left-to-right pipeline: relative input error, elasticity, relative output error. Display the approximation $\Delta f/f\approx E(x)\Delta x/x$. Include the power-function example $E=n$ in a separate lower strip. The example must say ``approximately'' and should not imply that finite percentage changes are exact.

\textbf{Web interaction.} Let users select models such as $x^2$, $x^3$, $e^x$, and $\ln x$, choose an operating point, and enter a small percentage perturbation. Compare the derivative prediction with the exact percentage change. Display both signed elasticity and its magnitude as a condition measure. Warn when the perturbation is too large for a local approximation.

\textbf{Accessibility and QA.} Alt text should narrate the multiplicative pipeline and power-function example. Equations must be available as MathML or accessible LaTeX. On mobile, stack the boxes. Verify unit cancellation, signs, and exact-versus-approximate readouts; test points where $f(x)=0$, where relative sensitivity is undefined and the interface must explain why.

visuals.title_latex: For a convex function, a stationary point is automatically global
visuals.caption_latex: A convex graph lies above each tangent line. When the tangent slope is zero, that horizontal line supports the entire graph from below, so no other point can have a smaller function value.
visuals.learning_purpose: This visual shows why convex optimization is unusually trustworthy. In ordinary optimization, a critical point is only a candidate. Under convexity, the tangent inequality converts a zero derivative into a global guarantee.
visuals.long_description: A convex graph lies above each tangent line. When the tangent slope is zero, that horizontal line supports the entire graph from below, so no other point can have a smaller function value. The horizontal green line touches the curve at the stationary point and stays below the graph everywhere shown. Convexity turns the local derivative statement f'(x *)=0 into the global conclusion f(x) f(x *) for every point in the interval.
visuals.reading_guide_latex: The horizontal green line touches the curve at the stationary point and stays below the graph everywhere shown. Convexity turns the local derivative statement $f'(x_*)=0$ into the global conclusion $f(x)\ge f(x_*)$ for every point in the interval.
visuals.editorial_brief_latex:
\textbf{Instructional purpose.} This visual shows why convex optimization is unusually trustworthy. In ordinary optimization, a critical point is only a candidate. Under convexity, the tangent inequality converts a zero derivative into a global guarantee.

\textbf{Exact composition.} Plot one clearly convex function with a unique minimum and its horizontal tangent at the minimizing point. The curve should remain visibly above the tangent across the full window. Label the stationary point, tangent, and inequality $f(y)\ge f(x_*)+f'(x_*)(y-x_*)=f(x_*)$. Avoid using a symmetric parabola as if symmetry were the reason; accompanying prose should name convexity.

\textbf{Web interaction.} Let the learner move the tangent point along a convex curve and observe that every tangent remains below the graph. Then switch to a nonconvex curve where a tangent may cross and a stationary point may fail to be global. A second toggle can compare $f''\ge0$ with an increasing derivative graph.

\textbf{Accessibility and QA.} Alt text should state the tangent-below-graph property and global-minimum conclusion. Use line pattern and labels in addition to color. Test the interaction at endpoints and flat intervals. On mobile, keep the inequality below the plot rather than overlapping it.

visuals.title_latex: Cauchy's theorem matches a ratio of secant changes to a ratio of instantaneous rates
visuals.caption_latex: For two functions on the same input interval, one interior point $c$ makes $[f(b)-f(a)]/[g(b)-g(a)]=f'(c)/g'(c)$. The same $c$ must be used in both derivative graphs.
visuals.learning_purpose: The paired plots should make Cauchy's theorem feel like a two-function version of the ordinary Mean Value Theorem. The crucial feature is that one shared point c produces the derivative ratio, not two unrelated points chosen separately.
visuals.long_description: For two functions on the same input interval, one interior point c makes [f(b)-f(a)]/[g(b)-g(a)]=f'(c)/g'(c) . The same c must be used in both derivative graphs. Both panels use the same input interval and the same interior point. For this example, the secant changes satisfy f/ g=8/2=4 , while the derivative ratio at c=2 is f'(2)/g'(2)=4/1=4 . The theorem compares two changing quantities rather than comparing either one directly with x .
visuals.reading_guide_latex: Both panels use the same input interval and the same interior point. For this example, the secant changes satisfy $\Delta f/\Delta g=8/2=4$, while the derivative ratio at $c=2$ is $f'(2)/g'(2)=4/1=4$. The theorem compares two changing quantities rather than comparing either one directly with $x$.
visuals.editorial_brief_latex:
\textbf{Instructional purpose.} The paired plots should make Cauchy's theorem feel like a two-function version of the ordinary Mean Value Theorem. The crucial feature is that one shared point $c$ produces the derivative ratio, not two unrelated points chosen separately.

\textbf{Mathematical specification.} Use $a=1$, $b=3$, $f(x)=x^2+1$, and $g(x)=x+1$. The secant changes are $8$ and $2$, and at $c=2$ the derivatives are $4$ and $1$. Mark corresponding endpoints and $c$ in both panels. Use one line style for secants and another for tangents; direct labels should identify the ratios.

\textbf{Web interaction.} Permit alternative pairs of functions satisfying the hypotheses. The learner moves $c$ and watches the derivative ratio until it matches the fixed secant-change ratio. A later reveal connects the construction to a $0/0$ quotient limit. The interface must prevent the misleading interpretation that $f/g=f'/g'$ pointwise.

\textbf{Accessibility and QA.} Alt text should list both functions, interval, changes, derivatives, and equality of ratios. Synchronize keyboard focus between corresponding points in the two panels. On mobile, stack the graphs and keep a shared $c$ slider. Verify all equations and axis limits; the left plot must include $f(3)=10$, so its vertical maximum must exceed the point rather than clipping it.
